claim: The paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) has been shown to be involved in defensive behaviors.
source: Both the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) have been shown to be involved in defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing PVN's role in defensive behaviors.

claim: The parabrachial nucleus (PBN) has been shown to be involved in defensive behaviors.
source: Both the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus (PVN) and the parabrachial nucleus (PBN) have been shown to be involved in defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing PBN's role in defensive behaviors.

claim: Cholecystokinin (CCK)-expressing neurons in the lateral PBN (LPBCCK) directly project to the PVN.
source: Here, by retrograde and anterograde tracing, we uncover that cholecystokinin (CCK)-expressing neurons in the lateral PBN (LPBCCK) directly project to the PVN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde and anterograde tracing experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: LPBCCK neurons actively respond to various threat stimuli.
source: By in vivo fiber photometry recording, we find that LPBCCK neurons actively respond to various threat stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo fiber photometry recording data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Selective photoactivation of LPBCCK neurons promotes aversion and defensive behaviors.
source: Selective photoactivation of LPBCCK neurons promotes aversion and defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data showing behavioral changes upon photoactivation.

claim: Photoinhibition of LPBCCK neurons attenuates rat or looming stimuli-induced flight responses.
source: Conversely, photoinhibition of LPBCCK neurons attenuates rat or looming stimuli-induced flight responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experimental data showing reduced flight responses.

claim: Optogenetic activation of LPBCCK axon terminals within the PVN promotes defensive behaviors.
source: Optogenetic activation of LPBCCK axon terminals within the PVN or PVN glutamatergic neurons promotes defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data showing behavioral changes upon terminal activation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PVN glutamatergic neurons promotes defensive behaviors.
source: Optogenetic activation of LPBCCK axon terminals within the PVN or PVN glutamatergic neurons promotes defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data showing behavioral changes upon PVN glutamatergic neuron activation.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of local PVN neurons prevents LPBCCK-PVN pathway activation-driven flight responses.
source: Whereas chemogenetic and pharmacological inhibition of local PVN neurons prevent LPBCCK-PVN pathway activation-driven flight responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic experimental data showing reduced flight responses upon PVN inhibition.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of local PVN neurons prevents LPBCCK-PVN pathway activation-driven flight responses.
source: Whereas chemogenetic and pharmacological inhibition of local PVN neurons prevent LPBCCK-PVN pathway activation-driven flight responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experimental data showing reduced flight responses upon PVN inhibition.

claim: LPBCCK neurons recruit downstream PVN neurons to actively engage in flight responses.
source: These data suggest that LPBCCK neurons recruit downstream PVN neurons to actively engage in flight responses.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined optogenetic activation and inhibition experiments showing the necessity of PVN for LPBCCK-driven behaviors.

claim: The LPBCCK-PVN pathway plays a previously unrecognized role in controlling defensive behaviors.
source: Our study identifies a previously unrecognized role for the LPBCCK-PVN pathway in controlling defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the novel findings presented in the manuscript regarding the LPBCCK-PVN pathway.

claim: Defensive behaviors are critical for animal survival.
source: Defensive behaviors are critical for animal's survival.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific consensus about the evolutionary importance of defensive behaviors.

claim: Defensive responses are generally divided into two categories: to avoid being discovered (such as freezing or hiding behaviors) or being caught (such as escaping or attacking behaviors).
source: From the perspective of predator and prey interactions, defensive responses are generally divided into two categories: to avoid being discovered (such as freezing or hiding behaviors) or being caught (such as escaping or attacking behaviors) (Crawford and Masterson, 1982; Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on defensive behavior categorization.

claim: Which type of defensive behavior is selected depends on many factors, including the intensity and proximity of the threat, as well as the surrounding context.
source: Which type of defensive behavior is selected depends on many factors, including the intensity and proximity of the threat, as well as the surrounding context.
evidence: This claim draws from established scientific knowledge about factors influencing defensive behavior selection.

claim: Escape is triggered when animals are faced with an imminent threat with a shelter nearby.
source: In general, escape is triggered when animals are faced with an imminent threat with a shelter nearby (Eilam, 2005; Lin et al., 2023; Perusini and Fanselow, 2015; Sun et al., 2020b; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on escape behavior triggers.

claim: Several brain regions, including the periaqueductal gray (PAG), amygdala, and medial hypothalamic zone (MHZ), have been implicated in mediating escape behaviors.
source: Several brain regions, including the periaqueductal gray (PAG), amygdala, and medial hypothalamic zone (MHZ), have been implicated in mediating escape behaviors (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2013; Tovote et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2021b; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on brain regions involved in escape behaviors.

claim: A subset of VMH neurons collaterally project to the AHN and PAG to promote both escape and avoidance behaviors.
source: For example, a subset of VMH neurons collaterally project to the AHN and PAG to promote both escape and avoidance behaviors (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on VMH neuron projections.

claim: PMd neurons project to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray region (dlPAG) and the anteromedial ventral thalamic region (AMV) to control escape behaviors.
source: Moreover, PMd neurons project to the dorsolateral periaqueductal gray region (dlPAG) and the anteromedial ventral thalamic region (AMV) also control escape behaviors (Wang et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PMd neuron projections.

claim: PVN, an area enriched with endocrine neurons, has been associated with escape behaviors.
source: In addition, PVN, an area enriched with endocrine neurons, has also been associated with escape behaviors (Mangieri et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PVN's role in escape behaviors.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Sim1+ neurons in the PVN triggers escape.
source: Optogenetic activation of Sim1+ neurons in the PVN triggers escape and projections from the PVN to both the ventral midbrain region (vMB) and the ventral lateral septum (LSv) mediate defensive-like behaviors, including hiding, escape jumping and hyperlocomotion (Mangieri et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN Sim1+ neuron activation effects.

claim: Projections from the PVN to both the ventral midbrain region (vMB) and the ventral lateral septum (LSv) mediate defensive-like behaviors, including hiding, escape jumping and hyperlocomotion.
source: Optogenetic activation of Sim1+ neurons in the PVN triggers escape and projections from the PVN to both the ventral midbrain region (vMB) and the ventral lateral septum (LSv) mediate defensive-like behaviors, including hiding, escape jumping and hyperlocomotion (Mangieri et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN projection effects.

claim: PBN serves as an important relay station for sensory transmission.
source: Located in the dorsolateral pons, PBN, serves as an important relay station for sensory transmission (Fulwiler and Saper, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PBN's role in sensory transmission.

claim: Electrical lesions of the PBN or local microinjections of kainic acid into the PBN induced defensive behaviors.
source: Electrical lesions of the PBN or local microinjections of kainic acid into the PBNinduced defensive behaviors (Mileikovskii and Verevkina, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PBN lesion effects.

claim: Exposure of the olfactory predator cue, trimethylthiazoline (TMT), increased c-fos expression in the LPB.
source: In addition, exposure of the olfactory predator cue, trimethylthiazoline (TMT), increased c-fos expression in the LPB (Day et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on TMT exposure effects on LPB.

claim: Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) neurons, located in the external lateral subnuclei of PBN (PBel), have been shown to mediate alarm responses and defensive behaviors under stressful or threatening circumstances via projections to the amygdala and the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST).
source: More importantly, calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) neurons, located in the external lateral subnuclei of PBN (PBel), have been shown to mediate alarm responses and defensive behaviors under stressful or threatening circumstances via projections to the amygdala and the bed nucleus of stria terminalis (BNST) ( Han et al., 2015a; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on CGRP neuron functions.

claim: Both CCK and CCK receptor-expressing neurons have been implicated in defensive behaviors.
source: Both CCK and CCK receptor-expressing neurons have been implicated in defensive behaviors (Bertoglio et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on CCK's role in defensive behaviors.

claim: PVN neurons express CCK receptors and are involved in defensive behaviors.
source: PVN neurons also express CCK receptors and are involved in defensive behaviors (Mangieri et al., 2019; O'Shea and Gundlach, 1993; Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN CCK receptor expression and function.

claim: The LPB is an important upstream CCKergic input to the PVN.
source: We injected the Cre-dependent retrograde tracer (AAV2-Retro-DIO-EYFP) into the PVN of Cck-cre mice and found that the LPB is an important upstream CCKergic input to the PVN.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: LPBCCK neurons were recruited upon exposure to various threat stimuli.
source: We further showed that LPBCCK neurons were recruited upon exposure to various threat stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo fiber photometry recording data.

claim: Optogenetic activation of either LPBCCK neuronal somas or their projections to the PVN promotes defensive responses.
source: Optogenetic activation of either LPBCCK neuronal somas or their projections to the PVN promotes defensive responses
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experimental data.

claim: Inhibition of LPBCCK neurons attenuates defensive-like behaviors.
source: whereas their inhibition attenuates defensive-like behaviors, suggesting an essential and sufficient role for LPBCCK-PVN pathway in mediating defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic inhibition experimental data.

claim: The LPBCCK-PVN pathway plays an essential and sufficient role in mediating defensive behaviors.
source: whereas their inhibition attenuates defensive-like behaviors, suggesting an essential and sufficient role for LPBCCK-PVN pathway in mediating defensive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined activation and inhibition experimental data.

claim: Abundant EYFP+ neurons were observed in the LPB, medial orbital cortex (MO), and cingulate cortex (CC) after retrograde tracing from PVN in Cck-cre mice.
source: We observed abundant EYFP+ neurons in the LPB, medial orbital cortex (MO), and cingulate cortex (CC), with scattered EYFP+ cells in the PAG and dysgranular insular cortex (DI) (Figure 1B–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing and shown in Figure 1B-H.

claim: Scattered EYFP+ cells were observed in the PAG and dysgranular insular cortex (DI) after retrograde tracing from PVN in Cck-cre mice.
source: We observed abundant EYFP+ neurons in the LPB, medial orbital cortex (MO), and cingulate cortex (CC), with scattered EYFP+ cells in the PAG and dysgranular insular cortex (DI) (Figure 1B–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing and shown in Figure 1B-H.

claim: LPB is a region critical for sensory signal processing.
source: Since LPB is a region critical for sensory signal processing, we mainly focused on the LPB in the following study (Fulwiler and Saper, 1984; Garfield et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LPB's role in sensory processing.

claim: LPBCCK neurons (84.0% ± 1.7%) predominantly expressed Slc17a6.
source: We found that LPBCCK neurons (84.0% ± 1.7%) predominantly expressed Slc17a6, with a tiny subpopulation (2.0% ± 1.2%) expressing Slc32a1, suggesting that LPBCCK neurons were mostly glutamatergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: A tiny subpopulation (2.0% ± 1.2%) of LPBCCK neurons expressed Slc32a1.
source: We found that LPBCCK neurons (84.0% ± 1.7%) predominantly expressed Slc17a6, with a tiny subpopulation (2.0% ± 1.2%) expressing Slc32a1, suggesting that LPBCCK neurons were mostly glutamatergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: LPBCCK neurons were mostly glutamatergic neurons.
source: We found that LPBCCK neurons (84.0% ± 1.7%) predominantly expressed Slc17a6, with a tiny subpopulation (2.0% ± 1.2%) expressing Slc32a1, suggesting that LPBCCK neurons were mostly glutamatergic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the in situ hybridization data showing high Slc17a6 expression.

claim: Minimal co-localization (2.2% ± 0.37%) was observed between CCK and CGRP in the LPB.
source: In addition, co-labeling with another neuropeptide, CGRP, revealed minimal co-localization (2.2% ± 0.37%) between CCK and CGRP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G), suggesting primary separation between these two subpopulations of neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-labeling experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G.

claim: There is primary separation between CCK and CGRP neuronal subpopulations in the LPB.
source: In addition, co-labeling with another neuropeptide, CGRP, revealed minimal co-localization (2.2% ± 0.37%) between CCK and CGRP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–G), suggesting primary separation between these two subpopulations of neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the minimal co-localization data.

claim: LPBCCK neurons comprise predominantly glutamatergic neurons, which barely overlap with CGRP neurons.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that LPBCCK neurons comprise predominantly glutamatergic neurons, which barely overlap with CGRP neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined in situ hybridization and co-labeling data.

claim: Prominent GFP+ fibers and mRuby+ bouton-like structures, reminiscent of axonal terminals, were observed within the PVN after anterograde tracing from LPBCCK neurons.
source: We observed prominent GFP+ fibers and mRuby+ bouton-like structures, reminiscent of axonal terminals, within the PVN (Figure 1K) and other brain regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Light stimulation-induced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs), rather than inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), were successfully recorded from PVN neurons upon optogenetic stimulation of LPBCCK axonal terminals.
source: We successfully recorded light stimulation-induced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs), rather than inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data from brain slice recordings.

claim: EPSCs induced by optogenetic stimulation of LPBCCK axonal terminals were blocked in the presence of TTX, but rescued by 4-AP.
source: These EPSCs were blocked in the presence of the sodium channel antagonist tetrodotoxin (TTX), but rescued by the potassium channel antagonist 4-Aminopyridine (4-AP) (Figure 1M–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1M–N.

claim: NMDA receptor antagonist AP5 and AMPA receptor antagonist CNQX blocked light stimulation-induced EPSCs from LPBCCK terminals to PVN neurons.
source: Further, NMDA receptor antagonist AP5, and AMPA receptor antagonist CNQX also blocked light stimulation-induced EPSCs (Figure 1O–P), validating that PVN neurons receive monosynaptic excitatory innervations from LPBCCK neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1O–P.

claim: PVN neurons receive monosynaptic excitatory innervations from LPBCCK neurons.
source: Further, NMDA receptor antagonist AP5, and AMPA receptor antagonist CNQX also blocked light stimulation-induced EPSCs (Figure 1O–P), validating that PVN neurons receive monosynaptic excitatory innervations from LPBCCK neurons.
evidence: This claim is validated by the combined electrophysiology data with TTX, 4-AP, AP5, and CNQX.

claim: LPBCCK neurons have been shown to regulate glucose homeostasis and body temperature.
source: LPBCCK neurons have been shown to regulate glucose homeostasis and body temperature (Garfield et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LPBCCK neuron functions.

claim: 5–20 Hz blue laser pulses induced time-locked action potential firing in ChR2-expressing LPBCCK neurons, with 20 Hz inducing maximal firing capacities.
source: We observed that 5–20 Hz blue laser pulses induced time-locked action potential firing, with 20 Hz inducing maximal firing capacities. We then chose 20 Hz for the following in vivo stimulation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons significantly reduced the duration of mice in the laser-paired chamber in the RTPA test.
source: We found that activation of LPBCCK neurons significantly reduced the duration of mice in the laser-paired chamber, accompanied by rapid running or flight to the other laser-unpaired chamber, indicating an obvious aversion-like avoidance and/or fear-related defensive-like behaviors (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the RTPA test shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons was accompanied by rapid running or flight to the laser-unpaired chamber in the RTPA test.
source: We found that activation of LPBCCK neurons significantly reduced the duration of mice in the laser-paired chamber, accompanied by rapid running or flight to the other laser-unpaired chamber, indicating an obvious aversion-like avoidance and/or fear-related defensive-like behaviors (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the RTPA test shown in Figure 2F–G.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons indicates aversion-like avoidance and/or fear-related defensive-like behaviors.
source: We found that activation of LPBCCK neurons significantly reduced the duration of mice in the laser-paired chamber, accompanied by rapid running or flight to the other laser-unpaired chamber, indicating an obvious aversion-like avoidance and/or fear-related defensive-like behaviors (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data in the RTPA test.

claim: Activating LPBCCK neurons induced robust flight-to-nest behavior in mice, with much shorter latency and faster speed running towards the nest.
source: Of note, activating LPBCCK neurons induced robust flight-to-nest behavior in mice, with much shorter latency and faster speed running towards the nest (latency: EYFP, 87.71 ± 22.38 s vs. ChR2, 7.571 ± 0.8123 s; speed: EYFP, 184.4% ± 30.4% vs. ChR2, 361.7% ± 31.5%), followed by longer stay in the nest (EYFP, 63.906% ± 3.645% vs. ChR2, 97.26% ± 2.737%; Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the flight-to-nest test shown in Figure 2I–K.

claim: Activating LPBCCK neurons was followed by longer stay in the nest in the flight-to-nest test.
source: Of note, activating LPBCCK neurons induced robust flight-to-nest behavior in mice, with much shorter latency and faster speed running towards the nest (latency: EYFP, 87.71 ± 22.38 s vs. ChR2, 7.571 ± 0.8123 s; speed: EYFP, 184.4% ± 30.4% vs. ChR2, 361.7% ± 31.5%), followed by longer stay in the nest (EYFP, 63.906% ± 3.645% vs. ChR2, 97.26% ± 2.737%; Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the flight-to-nest test shown in Figure 2I–K.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons induces aversion-like avoidance and defensive-like flight-to-nest behaviors.
source: These data suggest that activation of LPBCCK neurons induces aversion-like avoidance and defensive-like flight-to-nest behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined RTPA and flight-to-nest behavioral data.

claim: Defensive behaviors are usually accompanied by changes in the autonomic nervous system, such as increased heart rates, dilated pupil size and elevated cortisol levels.
source: Defensive behaviors are usually accompanied by changes in the autonomic nervous system, such as increased heart rates, dilated pupil size and elevated cortisol levels (Dong et al., 2019; Gross and Canteras, 2012; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on autonomic changes during defensive behaviors.

claim: Photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons significantly increased heart rates.
source: We found that photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons also significantly increased heart rates and enlarged pupil diameters, along with elevated plasma levels of corticosterone (Figure 2L–P)
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 2L–P.

claim: Photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons enlarged pupil diameters.
source: We found that photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons also significantly increased heart rates and enlarged pupil diameters, along with elevated plasma levels of corticosterone (Figure 2L–P)
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 2L–P.

claim: Photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons elevated plasma levels of corticosterone.
source: We found that photostimulation of LPBCCK neurons also significantly increased heart rates and enlarged pupil diameters, along with elevated plasma levels of corticosterone (Figure 2L–P)
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 2L–P.

claim: Activating LPBCCK neurons induces fast sympathetic changes, leading to an arousal state accompanying the defensive responses in mice.
source: suggesting that activating LPBCCK neurons induces fast sympathetic changes, leading to an arousal state accompanying the defensive responses in mice (Salay et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the physiological changes observed and supported by citation.

claim: Long-term fear may trigger anxiety-like states in animals.
source: Since activation of LPBCCK neurons induced fear-associated flight-to-nest behaviors and long-term fear may trigger anxiety-like states in animals (Tovote et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on fear and anxiety relationships.

claim: After 10 min of light stimulation, mice injected with ChR2 exhibited significantly reduced center time and center entries in the open field tests without affecting total distance.
source: After 10 min of light stimulation, mice injected with ChR2 exhibited significantly reduced center time and center entries in the open field tests without affecting total distance, and decreased open arm entries and time in the elevated plus maze tests (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–J)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from open field tests shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–J.

claim: After 10 min of light stimulation, mice injected with ChR2 exhibited decreased open arm entries and time in the elevated plus maze tests.
source: After 10 min of light stimulation, mice injected with ChR2 exhibited significantly reduced center time and center entries in the open field tests without affecting total distance, and decreased open arm entries and time in the elevated plus maze tests (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–J)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from elevated plus maze tests shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–J.

claim: Prolonged activation of LPBCCK neurons induces anxiety-like behaviors in mice.
source: suggesting that prolonged activation of LPBCCK neurons also induces anxiety-like behaviors in mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data in open field and elevated plus maze tests.

claim: LPB neurons were shown to be activated when animals are in proximity to dangerous stimuli.
source: LPB neurons were shown to be activated when animals are in proximity to dangerous stimuli (Campos et al., 2018; Day et al., 2004; Han et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LPB neuron activation.

claim: Elevated calcium responses of LPBCCK neurons were observed by heat stimuli (43 °C).
source: Consistent with previous observation (Yang et al., 2020), we observed elevated calcium responses of LPBCCK neurons by heat stimuli (43 °C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D and citation to prior work.

claim: The calcium signals of LPBCCK neurons gradually rise when mice approached the rat in the predator-exposure assay.
source: We observed that the calcium signals of LPBCCK neurons gradually rise when mice approached the rat.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data from the rat exposure assay.

claim: At the moment of escape initiation, when mice turned back and dashed away from the rat, the calcium signals of LPBCCK neurons reached a peak.
source: At the moment of escape initiation, when mice turned back and dashed away from the rat, the calcium signals reached a peak (Figure 3D–G and L).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3D–G and L.

claim: The calcium signals of LPBCCK neurons ramped down as mice gained distance from the rat.
source: However, the signals ramped down as mice gained distance from the rat.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data from the rat exposure assay.

claim: Activities of LPBCCK neurons were unaffected in the presence of a toy rat.
source: Notably, activities of LPBCCK neurons were unaffected in the presence of a toy rat (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–H.

claim: LPBCCK neurons showed increased calcium signals in the looming assay.
source: In the presence of the visual predatory cue, such as appearing and expanding looming shadows to mimic an approaching predator (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013), LPBCCK neurons also showed increased calcium signals (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3H and citation to prior work on looming stimuli.

claim: In the looming assay, the elevated calcium signals of LPBCCK neurons reached peak when the animal initiated escape, but reduced once it ran into the nest.
source: Similar to rat exposure assay, we also tested the response of these neurons in the looming assay, the elevated calcium signals reached peak when the animal initiated escape, but reduced once it ran into the nest (Figure 3H–K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3H–K and M.

claim: LPBCCK neurons showed elevated calcium signals when mice were exposed to the olfactory predatory cue, TMT odor.
source: LPBCCK neurons also showed elevated calcium signals when mice were exposed to the olfactory predatory cue, TMT odor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1–L.

claim: The elevation of the calcium signal in LPBCCK neurons was correlated with the onset of escape responses.
source: Correlative analysis revealed that the elevation of the calcium signal was correlated with the onset of escape responses (Figure 3N–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlative analysis data shown in Figure 3N–O.

claim: Threatening stimuli of different sensory predatory cue stimulated the LPBCCK neurons.
source: Thus, threatening stimuli of different sensory predatory cue stimulated the LPBCCK neurons (Figure 3P–R).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined fiber photometry data across different threat stimuli shown in Figure 3P–R.

claim: LPBCCK neurons encode innate threat stimuli-evoked aversion and flight behaviors.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that LPBCCK neurons encode innate threat stimuli-evoked aversion and flight behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined fiber photometry data showing LPBCCK neuron responses to various threat stimuli.

claim: Optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons significantly increased the time and entries of mice to the danger zone in the rat exposure test.
source: However, optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons significantly increased the time (EYFP, 7.247% ± 2.329% vs. GtACR1, 26.57% ± 5.375%) and entries (EYFP, 6.167 ± 1.579 vs. GtACR1, 12.67 ± 2.141) of mice to the danger zone, with no effect on total travel distance (EYFP, 8.837 ± 1.934 m vs. GtACR1, 12.69 ± 1.421 m), suggesting a delayed flight response (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the rat exposure test shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: Optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons had no effect on total travel distance in the rat exposure test.
source: However, optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons significantly increased the time (EYFP, 7.247% ± 2.329% vs. GtACR1, 26.57% ± 5.375%) and entries (EYFP, 6.167 ± 1.579 vs. GtACR1, 12.67 ± 2.141) of mice to the danger zone, with no effect on total travel distance (EYFP, 8.837 ± 1.934 m vs. GtACR1, 12.69 ± 1.421 m), suggesting a delayed flight response (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the rat exposure test shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: Optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons suggests a delayed flight response in the rat exposure test.
source: However, optic inhibition of LPBCCK neurons significantly increased the time (EYFP, 7.247% ± 2.329% vs. GtACR1, 26.57% ± 5.375%) and entries (EYFP, 6.167 ± 1.579 vs. GtACR1, 12.67 ± 2.141) of mice to the danger zone, with no effect on total travel distance (EYFP, 8.837 ± 1.934 m vs. GtACR1, 12.69 ± 1.421 m), suggesting a delayed flight response (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing increased time and entries to the danger zone.

claim: Inhibition of LPBCCK neurons increased the latency fleeing to the nest in the looming test.
source: In the looming test (Figure 4I–J), inhibition of LPBCCK neurons also increased the latency fleeing to the nest (EYFP, 10.18 ± 2.828 s vs. GtACR1, 27.14 ± 6.526 s), followed by reduced hiding time in the nest (EYFP, 85.36% ± 9.846% vs. GtACR1, 39.17% ± 16.36%; Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the looming test shown in Figure 4I–J and 4K–L.

claim: Inhibition of LPBCCK neurons reduced hiding time in the nest in the looming test.
source: In the looming test (Figure 4I–J), inhibition of LPBCCK neurons also increased the latency fleeing to the nest (EYFP, 10.18 ± 2.828 s vs. GtACR1, 27.14 ± 6.526 s), followed by reduced hiding time in the nest (EYFP, 85.36% ± 9.846% vs. GtACR1, 39.17% ± 16.36%; Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the looming test shown in Figure 4I–J and 4K–L.

claim: LPBCCK neurons are required for proper defensive behaviors to rat exposure and looming stimuli.
source: Our data suggest that LPBCCK neurons are required for proper defensive behaviors to rat exposure and looming stimuli.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic inhibition data showing impaired defensive behaviors.

claim: Photostimulating the axonal terminals of LPBCCK neurons within the PVN induced shorter latency, faster speed running towards the nest, and longer stay in the nest.
source: By photostimulating the axonal terminals of LPBCCK neurons within the PVN, we also observed shorter latency (EYFP, 73.43 ± 21.08 s vs. ChR2, 8 ± 1.047 s), faster speed (EYFP, 122.3% ± 17.81% vs. ChR2, 277.9% ± 32.85%) running towards the nest, and longer stay in the nest, (EYFP, 3.751% ± 1.23% vs. ChR2, 89.29% ± 10.71%; Figure 5F–H), similar to soma activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from terminal activation shown in Figure 5F–H.

claim: Terminal activation of LPBCCK-PVN pathway increased heart rates.
source: As well, terminal activation also increased heart rates (Figure 5K) and plasma corticosterone levels (Figure 5N), but with no effects on pupil size (Figure 5L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Terminal activation of LPBCCK-PVN pathway increased plasma corticosterone levels.
source: As well, terminal activation also increased heart rates (Figure 5K) and plasma corticosterone levels (Figure 5N), but with no effects on pupil size (Figure 5L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Terminal activation of LPBCCK-PVN pathway had no effects on pupil size.
source: As well, terminal activation also increased heart rates (Figure 5K) and plasma corticosterone levels (Figure 5N), but with no effects on pupil size (Figure 5L–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological measurement data shown in Figure 5L–M.

claim: Activation of the LPBCCK-PVN pathway is sufficient to trigger flight-to-nest behavior, along with increased heart rates and corticosterone levels.
source: Together, these data suggest that activation of the LPBCCK-PVN pathway is sufficient to trigger flight-to-nest behavior, along with increased heart rates and corticosterone levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined behavioral and physiological data from terminal activation experiments.

claim: Upon CNO administration to inhibit PVN neurons, mice showed much longer latency, lower speed in returning to the nest, and reduced hiding time in the nest during LPBCCK terminal activation.
source: Upon CNO administration to inhibit PVN neurons, we observed a much longer latency, lower speed of the mice in returning to the nest, and reduced hiding time in the nest (latency: saline, 8.286 ± 1.475 s vs. CNO, 18.29 ± 2.843 s; speed: saline, 289.3% ± 25.22% vs. CNO, 124.7% ± 13.67%; time in the nest: saline, 81.55% ± 11.16% vs. CNO, 25.83% ± 10.32%; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from chemogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: The PVN is a required downstream target for LPBCCK neurons activation-induced defensive behavior.
source: These data suggest that the PVN is a required downstream target for LPBCCK neurons activation-induced defensive behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the chemogenetic inhibition data showing that PVN inhibition blocks LPBCCK-induced behaviors.

claim: Blocking glutamate receptors induced a longer latency, slower speed in returning to the nest, along with reduced hiding time in the nest during LPBCCK terminal activation.
source: We found that blocking glutamate receptors induced a longer latency, slower speed in returning to the nest, along with reduced hiding time in the nest (Figure 6I–K), when compared with ACSF-treated mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 6I–K.

claim: Blocking CCK receptors showed no significant effects on LPBCCK terminal activation-induced behaviors.
source: However, blocking CCK receptors showed no significant effects (Figure 6I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological manipulation data shown in Figure 6I–K.

claim: Glutamatergic transmission from LPBCCK neurons to the PVN mediates defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior.
source: These results suggest that glutamatergic transmission from LPBCCK neurons to the PVN mediates defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pharmacological data showing that glutamate receptor blockade, but not CCK receptor blockade, impairs behaviors.

claim: PVN neurons are mostly glutamatergic.
source: Of note, PVN neurons are mostly glutamatergic (Vong et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN neuron types.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PVNVglut2 neurons induced flight-to-nest behavior with shorter latency, faster speed, and longer hiding time in the nest.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of PVNVglut2 neurons also induced flight-to-nest behavior (latency: EYFP, 127.5 ± 22.5 s vs. ChR2, 12.83 ± 2.937 s; speed: EYFP, 142.4 ± 32.07% vs. ChR2, 384.4% ± 83.52%), followed by longer hiding time in the nest (EYFP, 0.2783% ± 0.2783% vs. ChR2, 61.11% ± 17.58%) (Figure 6N–P), compared to the control.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 6N–P.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PVNVglut2 neurons was sufficient to evoke defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior.
source: These data suggest that optogenetic activation of PVNVglut2 neurons was sufficient to evoke defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the optogenetic activation data showing robust flight-to-nest behavior.

claim: PVNCRH neurons have been shown to predict the occurrence of defensive behaviors in mice.
source: PVNCRH neurons have recently been shown to predict the occurrence of defensive behaviors in mice (Daviu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PVNCRH neuron functions.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the LPBCCK-PVN pathway primarily activated PVNCRH neurons, rather than vasopressin or oxytocin neurons.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic activation of the LPBCCK-PVN pathway primarily activated PVNCRH neurons, rather than vasopressin or oxytocin neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-fos staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PVNCRH neurons was not sufficient to drive defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior.
source: However, optogenetic activation of PVNCRH neurons was not sufficient to drive defensive-like flight-to-nest behavior (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–K; latency: EYFP, 77 ± 20.69 s vs. ChR2, 90.17 ± 22.03 s; speed: EYFP, 156.6 ± 22.59% vs. ChR2, 217.2% ± 61.54%; time in the nest: EYFP, 20.95% ± 13.89% vs. ChR2, 35.28% ± 20.48%).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–K.

claim: Hippocampal and cortical CCK-expressing neurons have been thought of mainly GABAergic.
source: Hippocampal and cortical CCK-expressing neurons have been thought of mainly GABAergic (Liu et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2020a; Whissell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on CCK neuron types in hippocampus and cortex.

claim: LPBCCK neurons are predominantly glutamatergic, similar to those in the amygdala.
source: We found that LPBCCK neurons are predominantly glutamatergic, similar to those in the amygdala (Shen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and citation to prior work on amygdala CCK neurons.

claim: The roles of LPBCGRP neurons have been associated with the passive defensive responses.
source: While the roles of LPBCGRP neurons have been associated with the passive defensive responses (Han et al., 2015b; Keay and Bandler, 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LPBCGRP neuron functions.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons primarily triggers active defensive responses, such as flight-to-nest behavior.
source: we show that activation of LPBCCK neurons primarily triggers active defensive responses, such as flight-to-nest behavior (Keay and Bandler, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data from optogenetic activation experiments and citation.

claim: CGRP and CCK neurons are spatially segregated in the LPB.
source: The fact that CGRP and CCK neurons are spatially segregated, responsive to distinct threat signals and involved in different defensive responses, indicating that LPB acts as an important integration center or hub to gate defensive responses when animals encounter different threats (Liu et al., 2022; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-labeling data showing minimal overlap and citations.

claim: CGRP and CCK neurons are responsive to distinct threat signals.
source: The fact that CGRP and CCK neurons are spatially segregated, responsive to distinct threat signals and involved in different defensive responses, indicating that LPB acts as an important integration center or hub to gate defensive responses when animals encounter different threats (Liu et al., 2022; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the discussion of CGRP and CCK neuron differences and supported by citations.

claim: CGRP and CCK neurons are involved in different defensive responses.
source: The fact that CGRP and CCK neurons are spatially segregated, responsive to distinct threat signals and involved in different defensive responses, indicating that LPB acts as an important integration center or hub to gate defensive responses when animals encounter different threats (Liu et al., 2022; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral data showing different responses and citations.

claim: LPB acts as an important integration center or hub to gate defensive responses when animals encounter different threats.
source: The fact that CGRP and CCK neurons are spatially segregated, responsive to distinct threat signals and involved in different defensive responses, indicating that LPB acts as an important integration center or hub to gate defensive responses when animals encounter different threats (Liu et al., 2022; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on CGRP and CCK neurons and supported by citations.

claim: LPBCCK neurons increase firing upon exposure to predators and/or predatory cues, which occurs before the initiation of an escape behavior.
source: In vivo calcium imaging showed that LPBCCK neurons increase firing upon exposure to predators and/or predatory cues, which occurs before the initiation of an escape behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by fiber photometry data showing calcium signal increases before escape.

claim: LPBCCK neurons may produce a preparatory signal before the escape initiation.
source: These findings indicate that LPBCCK neurons may produce a preparatory signal before the escape initiation, which allows the downstream targets to further assess the threat signals, plan escape routes and take appropriate motor actions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of calcium signal increases relative to escape initiation.

claim: LPBCCK neurons receive inputs from both the peripheral and visceral sensory system.
source: LPBCCK neurons are well positioned to play such an important role in linking the imminent threat to escape initiation, as they receive inputs from both the peripheral and visceral sensory system and project to many brain regions involved in defensive responses including the hypothalamus, PVT and PAG (Cooper and Blumstein, 2015; Ellard and Eller, 2009; Han et al., 2015b; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Saper and Loewy, 1980; Sun et al., 2020b; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on LPBCCK neuron inputs.

claim: LPBCCK neurons project to many brain regions involved in defensive responses including the hypothalamus, PVT and PAG.
source: LPBCCK neurons are well positioned to play such an important role in linking the imminent threat to escape initiation, as they receive inputs from both the peripheral and visceral sensory system and project to many brain regions involved in defensive responses including the hypothalamus, PVT and PAG (Cooper and Blumstein, 2015; Ellard and Eller, 2009; Han et al., 2015b; Krout and Loewy, 2000; Saper and Loewy, 1980; Sun et al., 2020b; Tokita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data and citations to prior literature.

claim: PVNCRH or PAGCCK neurons have been shown to be recruited during flight, with their peak activity occurring during flight rather than at flight initiation.
source: While PVNCRH or PAGCCK neurons have also been shown to be recruited during flight, their peak activity did not match the flight initiation, but occurred during flight (Daviu et al., 2020; La-Vu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVNCRH and PAGCCK neuron activity patterns.

claim: The peak activities of LPBCCK neurons at the onset of escape suggest that LPBCCK neurons likely gate and instruct the escape rather than directly control locomotive behaviors.
source: The peak activities of LPBCCK neurons at the onset of escape suggest that LPBCCK neurons likely gate and instruct the escape rather than directly control locomotive behaviors.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of LPBCCK neuron activity relative to escape initiation.

claim: Direct projections from the brainstem to the hypothalamus for the escape responses may be more conducive to escape in emergency situations.
source: Direct projections from the brainstem to the hypothalamus for the escape responses may be more conducive to escape in emergency situations.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the functional significance of the LPBCCK-PVN pathway.

claim: LPBCCK neurons project to the PVT, VMH and PAG, which have been associated with aversion and/or defensive behaviors.
source: Besides the PVN, we also observed that LPBCCK neurons project to the PVT, VMH and PAG, which have also been associated with aversion and/or defensive behaviors (LeDoux, 2012; Vianna et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data and citations to prior literature.

claim: PVN is important for neuroendocrine and autonomous regulation.
source: PVN is important for neuroendocrine and autonomous regulation (Canteras et al., 2001; Coote, 2005; Ferguson et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN functions.

claim: Earlier c-fos staining analyses suggest that PVN neurons are activated in response to different threat stimuli.
source: While earlier c-fos staining analyses suggest that PVN neurons are activated in response to different threat stimuli (Canteras et al., 2001; Faturi et al., 2014; Martinez et al., 2008; Staples et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN neuron activation.

claim: PVN neurons play important roles in defensive behaviors independent of hormonal actions.
source: Increasing evidence has demonstrated that PVN neurons play important roles in defensive behaviors independent of hormonal actions (Daviu et al., 2020; Mangieri et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on PVN neuron behavioral functions.

claim: Photoactivation of PVNSim1 neurons induced defensive responses.
source: Sim1, as a specific marker of PVN, studies have reported that photoactivation of PVNSim1 neurons induced defensive responses (Mangieri et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PVNSim1 neuron activation effects.

claim: Stimulating the LPBCCK-PVN pathway promoted flight-to-nest behaviors but activating PVNCRH neurons did not induce apparent flight-to-nest behaviors.
source: Intriguingly, stimulating the LPBCCK-PVN pathway promoted flight-to-nest behaviors but activating of PVNCRH neurons did not induce apparent flight-to-nest behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined optogenetic data from LPBCCK-PVN pathway and PVNCRH neuron activation experiments.

claim: Activation of the PVNCRH neurons have been shown to induce aversion.
source: Since PVNCRH neurons receive multiple inputs and activation of the PVNCRH neurons have been shown to induce aversion (Kim et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on PVNCRH neuron activation effects.

claim: Activation of LPBCCK neurons drives aversion, defensive and anxiety-like behaviors, evoking an arousal and stressed states.
source: Our data show that activation of LPBCCK neurons drives aversion, defensive and anxiety-like behaviors, evoking an arousal and stressed states.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined behavioral and physiological data from optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Fear, anxiety and stress responses are closely associated with mental illnesses with dysregulated neural circuits.
source: Fear, anxiety and stress responses are closely associated with mental illnesses with dysregulated neural circuits (Blanchard et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature on mental illness and neural circuits.
